{{short description|Swedish mathematician}}
'''Sonja Lyttkens''' (26 August 1919 – 18 December 2014){{r|kp}} was a Swedish mathematician, the third woman to earn a mathematics doctorate in Sweden and the first of these women to obtain a permanent university position in mathematics.{{r|ecm}} She is also known for her work to make academia less hostile to women,{{r|uu}} and for pointing out that the Swedish taxation system of the time, which provided an income deduction for husbands of non-working wives, pressured women even in low-income families not to work. Her observations helped push Sweden into taxing married people separately from their spouses.{{r|pif|nyberg}}

==Education and career==
[[File:Sonja Lyttkens.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Sonja Lyttkens]]
Lyttkens grew up in [[Halmstad]] and [[Karlskrona]], and moved to [[Kalmar]] in 1930. She moved again to Uppsala in 1937 to study mathematics, but her studies were interrupted by marriage and children.{{r|unt}} She earned a [[Licentiate (degree)|licentiate]] in 1951,{{r|unt}} and completed her Ph.D. at [[Uppsala University]] in 1956. Her dissertation, ''The Remainder In Tauberian Theorems'', concerned [[Abelian and Tauberian theorems|Tauberian theorems]] and was jointly supervised by [[Arne Beurling]] and [[Lennart Carleson]].{{r|mg}} She was the third woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics in Sweden, after [[Louise Petrén-Overton]] in 1911 and Ingrid Lindström in 1947.{{r|ecm}}

Although [[Sofya Kovalevskaya]] had become a full professor of mathematics in  a private university in Stockholm in 1884,{{r|sk}} women were forbidden from holding public university positions in Sweden until 1925,{{r|sk|uu}} and both Petrén and Lindström became schoolteachers.{{r|ecm}} Lyttkens obtained a permanent position as a senior lecturer at Uppsala University in 1963,{{r|ecm|uu}} and in 1970 she became the university's first female [[inspektor]] (an honorary chair of a student union), for the [[Kalmar nation, Uppsala|Kalmar nation]].{{r|uu}} She retired in 1984.{{r|kp}}

==Personal life==
Lyttkens was the daughter of Swedish sculptor [[Anna Petrus]] and her husband, physician Harald Lyttkens. Two of her children, {{ill|Ulla Lyttkens|se}} and [[Harald Hamrell]], both became film actors and directors.{{r|unt}}

As well as working in mathematics, Lyttkens also painted [[watercolor]]s before and after her retirement, and had several exhibitions of her paintings.{{r|kp}}
